title: Opinion | Why the NPL can turn Nepal’s promises into wins - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Why the NPL can turn Nepal’s promises into wins  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal is an emerging cricketing nation. Its players have challenged established teams, its supporters bring extraordinary passion, and businesses are increasingly backing the sport. The Nepal Premier League can bring these strengths together, laying the foundation for sustained international success.

The next step is to turn promise into victories.

Nepal’s recent World Cup appearances have shown both its potential and the work ahead. It pushed England close at the 2026 T20 World Cup and defeated Scotland, but heavy losses against Italy and West Indies exposed inconsistency. Sustaining its best cricket across a tournament remains the challenge.

Nepal has a strong base to build upon. Sandeep Lamichhane’s leg-spin, Dipendra Singh Airee’s all-round ability, Rohit Paudel’s batting and Sompal Kami’s seam bowling give Nepal players who can shape international contests. Airee and Kami were central to the victory over Scotland, showing what experienced players can achieve together.

The emerging talent is equally encouraging. Gulshan Jha’s match-winning bowling against Oman, Lokesh Bam’s fearless hitting against England and the wicket breakthroughs provided by Sher Malla and Nandan Yadav reveal a widening talent pool. These players need opportunities, patient development and greater exposure to demanding cricket.

NPL can provide precisely that. Sharing dressing rooms with experienced internationals offers lessons in preparation, tactics and responding to setbacks. Young players can observe how established professionals assess a situation, change their approach and retain composure when a match turns against them.

But exposure is not enough. Learning requires responsibility. Franchises must give emerging Nepali cricketers meaningful roles: bowling a difficult over, rebuilding an innings or finishing a chase. These experiences can help prepare the national team to win the key moments in international matches.

That brings us to mental conditioning.

Against South Africa at the 2024 T20 World Cup, Nepal lost by a single run. Against England in 2026, the margin was four. Both performances earned admiration, but they also revealed the thin, painful line between unsettling a powerful opponent and delivering the final blow.

Results alone cannot reveal players’ thoughts, and technical execution matters enormously. Yet composure, confidence and decision-making under pressure deserve the same structured attention as batting, bowling and fielding.

The mind, too, has to be trained.

The Cricket Association of Nepal should make specialist mental conditioning a regular part of preparation. Paddy Upton’s work with India’s 2011 World Cup-winning cricket team and its men’s hockey programme illustrates the value of such expertise across sports. Handling pressure, trusting preparation and recovering after mistakes must become practised skills.

Nepal has shown it can hold its nerve, including in a one-run victory over UAE during its successful qualification campaign for the 2026 T20 World Cup. The challenge is to reproduce that assurance consistently against stronger opposition. Its place in the next T20 World Cup, to be decided through the Global Qualifier, remains to be earned.

Meanwhile, an immediate opportunity awaits in fifty-over cricket. Kathmandu is scheduled to host the World Cup Qualifier Play-off in December, after the NPL ends. Four of eight teams will advance to the play-off. Home conditions and home support give Nepal a valuable edge.

The revised World Cup structure adds another incentive to aim high. The Qualifier winner enters the main group stage directly, while the other three qualifying teams must contest an opening tri-series for one remaining berth. Nepal must therefore prepare to win at every stage.

NPL’s growing support provides a strong platform. Its third-season opening attracted a near-capacity crowd. Siddhartha Bank, Arya Pharma, Omoda Jaecoo, Red Bull, Bajaj Pulsar, Asian Paints, VIVO and Nepal Telecom illustrate the breadth of commercial backing. Broadcast on Star Sports, FanCode and Himalaya Sports take the competition to wider audiences.

The passion was always there. The league has given it a platform for a bigger ambition.

The challenge now is to ensure that revenue and attention strengthen coaching, facilities, youth competitions and player welfare throughout the year. A successful league must leave behind better opportunities long after the final has been played.

Training grounds and pathways for young players must spread across the country. Kathmandu can be the centrepiece, but Nepal’s cricketing nursery must extend far beyond the capital.

title: 'Millions of children in Nepal facing overlapping climate, environmental, disaster risks' - The Rising Nepal
description: 'Millions of children in Nepal facing overlapping climate, environmental, disaster risks'  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By TRN Online, Kathmandu, Nov. 5: A new UNICEF advocacy brief launched today warns that millions of children in Nepal are facing escalating and overlapping climate, environmental and disaster risks that threaten their health, nutrition, education, protection and future prospects.

Based on analysis of multiple national and global data sources, the brief entitled Growing Up in a Climate Hotspot: The Risks Shaping the Lives and Futures of Nepal's Children, highlights how climate change is already reshaping childhood across Nepal and calls for urgent action to place children at the centre of climate policy, financing and action.

According to the UNICEF press release, the findings paint a stark picture: 9.9 million children are exposed to unhealthy levels of air pollution, making air pollution one of the most widespread environmental threats facing children in Nepal. 7.3 million children are exposed to drought, threatening water security, livelihoods, food production and nutrition. 5.7 million children are exposed to extreme hot days, with rising temperatures jeopardizing children's health, wellbeing and learning. 2.9 million children are exposed to rainfall-triggered landslides. An estimated 2.4 million children are exposed to multiple high-intensity climate hazards, compounding risks and making recovery more difficult.

The brief notes that climate change is not only increasing children's exposure to hazards but also placing growing pressure on the services they rely upon. While Nepal has made significant development gains, major vulnerabilities remain, read the press release.

Only 47.5 per cent of the population has access to safely managed drinking water, one in four children under five is stunted, 22 per cent of children live in multidimensional poverty, and climate-related shocks continue to increase risks of child labour, child marriage, disease outbreaks and learning disruption.

" The climate crisis is increasingly becoming a child rights crisis," said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. "Children have contributed least to climate change, yet they are among those bearing its greatest consequences. Every flood, drought, heatwave and pollution episode threatens children's health, nutrition, education and protection. As Nepal prepares to engage in global climate discussions at COP 31 , we have an opportunity and responsibility to ensure children are placed at the centre of climate action, climate finance and adaptation efforts."

The brief emphasizes that climate risks are not experienced equally. Children living in poverty, girls, children with disabilities, children from historically marginalized communities, and those living in remote and climate-vulnerable areas face disproportionately higher risks while having fewer resources to cope and recover.

In a significant step towards advancing child- and youth-responsive climate action, the Government of Nepal formally endorsed the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action during the National Climate Summit on 29 October.

The first-of-its-kind global declaration, launched at COP 25 and endorsed by 78 countries to date, commits governments to advancing climate action that responds to the rights, needs and contributions of children and young people. Building on Nepal's global recognition for having one of the world's most child-responsive climate plans, the signed Declaration will be formally handed over to UNICEF representatives at COP 31 in Türkiye, further showcasing Nepal's leadership in placing children and young people at the centre of climate policy and action.

Ahead of COP 31 , UNICEF Nepal is calling on:

The Government to integrate children's needs and rights across climate policies, adaptation plans, disaster risk reduction strategies and climate financing frameworks.

Governments, development partners and climate finance institutions to increase investments in child-responsive adaptation and loss and damage, including resilient health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection and social protection, with access approaches responsive to age, gender and disability

National and subnational governments to use disaggregated, child-focused climate risk evidence to guide planning and prioritize the most vulnerable communities.

The private sector to support climate-resilient infrastructure, clean energy solutions and innovations that protect children's wellbeing.

All stakeholders to ensure children and young people are meaningfully included in climate decision-making processes at local, national and global levels.

The brief also highlights the importance of listening to children and young people, who are already leading local climate action and advocating for stronger responses.

title: WTO flags Nepal’s weak manufacturing base and narrow export markets - The Kathmandu Post
description: WTO flags Nepal’s weak manufacturing base and narrow export markets  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal continues to grapple with poor infrastructure, high trade costs, weak production capacity, and limited export diversification, despite modernising customs and introducing policy reforms to attract investment, a recent review by the World Trade Organisation says.

According to the WTO Secretariat’s Trade Policy Review of Nepal, the country’s manufacturing sector contributes just 4.9 percent to gross domestic product, while around 68 percent of merchandise exports go to India. This points to Nepal’s heavy dependence on a single export market.

Although merchandise exports increased from $860 million in fiscal year 2018-19 to $1.5 billion in 2023, there has been little progress in diversifying export products and destinations, the report says.

The review also pointed to gaps in implementing trade facilitation measures. Only 13 percent of customs declarations are processed through the green channel, while 42 percent still go through the red channel, which requires physical inspection.

The WTO acknowledged Nepal’s efforts to introduce reforms, including amendments to the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, the E-commerce Act and customs modernisation initiatives. However, it stressed that effective implementation of these measures remains crucial to improving the country’s trade performance.

It stresses the need to expand domestic production capacity, diversify export products and destinations, strengthen trade logistics, and improve participation in regional and global value chains.

Nepal’s economy also remains heavily reliant on remittances equivalent to 25.3 percent of its GDP, while the merchandise trade deficit stands at 24.3 percent of GDP. The figures reflect the country’s dependence on imports to meet domestic consumption and production needs.

Speaking at the 10th Global Review of Aid for Trade at the WTO in Geneva last Thursday, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, director-general of the WTO, called on developing countries, including least-developed countries (LDCs) such as Nepal, to strengthen domestic reforms, production capacity and value addition to increase their share of global trade.

Nepal has received a total of $8.94 million in support from the Enhanced Integrated Framework (EIF), while securing $1.8 million in co-funding from the government, private sector, donors and development partners for trade-related projects.

The EIF is a global partnership dedicated to helping least-developed countries and recently graduated countries harness trade and investment for resilient, sustainable and transformative development.

Anchored at the WTO, the framework brings together LDC governments, funding partners, international agencies and the private sector to address systemic trade and investment constraints and expand opportunities for long-term development.

Addressing the opening plenary session, titled ‘20 Years. Better Trade. Better Lives’, Okonjo-Iweala said development assistance should move beyond financing infrastructure and focus on helping countries overcome domestic regulatory and institutional barriers, expand manufacturing, and improve their ability to compete in international markets.

She said that despite substantial aid for trade over the past two decades, the share of LDCs in global trade has remained stagnant at around 1 percent.

Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Akihiko Tanaka said Nepal and other developing countries should prioritise quality infrastructure, customs modernisation, and resilient supply chains to strengthen trade competitiveness and achieve long-term economic growth.

“Development cooperation should go beyond mobilising private investment and focus on building infrastructure, strengthening institutions and developing human resources to generate sustainable economic benefits,” he said.

Drawing on JICA’s experience in Africa, Tanaka said one-stop border posts had reduced border-crossing times by around 70 percent at 15 locations through simplified customs procedures, improved coordination, and training of customs officials.

He said developing countries should build their own institutional capacity rather than rely on external assistance to replace domestic systems.

Tanaka also stressed the need for diversifying and strengthening supply chains, particularly as pandemics, conflicts, and natural disasters have exposed vulnerabilities in global trade networks.

For landlocked countries like Nepal, these priorities are particularly important in addressing cross-border trade bottlenecks, high transportation costs, and disruptions caused by natural disasters.

He also called for stronger partnerships among governments, development banks, businesses, and private investors, alongside predictable trade rules, to help developing economies move up the production and manufacturing value chain.

For Nepal, the remarks underline the need to improve the domestic business environment, strengthen productive capacity, promote value-added exports, and address policy and infrastructure bottlenecks that have constrained its integration into global trade.

Matthias Cormann, secretary-general of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, called on developing countries, including Nepal, to attract greater private investment, improve digital connectivity, and strengthen trade-related institutions to benefit more from global markets.

“LDCs continue to account for only around 1 percent of global goods exports and 0.5 percent of services exports, despite two decades of development assistance. Public development finance should be used to mobilise private investment through guarantees, co-financing and blended finance, while ensuring investments create local jobs, skills and businesses,” he said.

title: Americans Top Nepal’s Visitor List in October, but Number of Nepali Americans Remains Unknown - nepyork
description: Americans Top Nepal’s Visitor List in October, but Number of Nepali Americans Remains Unknown  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
The United States became Nepal’s largest source of international visitors in October, as arrivals from the country rose more than 31 percent from a year earlier, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Nepal Tourism Board from Department of Immigration records.

Nepal received 132,814 international visitors in October, a 3.4 percent increase from 128,443 in the same month last year. The United States accounted for 17,437 visitors, or 13.13 percent of the total, moving ahead of India and China to become Nepal’s largest individual source country.

The shift marks a reversal from October 2025, when India led with 17,298 visitors, followed by the United States with 13,286. Arrivals from the United States increased by 4,151 over the year, while those from India fell by 5,201.

U.S. Arrivals Rise Sharply

Visitors from the United States increased 31.2 percent in October, from 13,286 a year earlier. The timing coincided with Dashain, Nepal’s major Hindu festival, and the fall holiday travel season in the United States, periods when many Nepali Americans may travel to visit family and friends. The tourism figures, however, do not identify visitors by ethnic background, so they do not establish how many of the U.S. arrivals were Nepali Americans.

Nepal’s Department of Immigration has been tracking some travelers of Nepali origin who enter the country using nonresident Nepali visas obtained through an NRN card or citizenship certificate. But those records do not capture the entire Nepali American population. Many Nepali Americans do not hold either document and instead travel on ordinary U.S. passports, entering Nepal on tourist visas and paying the applicable visa fees.

The Nepali American population in the United States is estimated to exceed 125,000, based on figures compiled from U.S. citizenship and population data. That estimate includes more than 100,000 naturalized Nepali immigrants as well as second-generation Nepali Americans born in the United States.

The Asian American Research Center estimated the Nepali American adult population at 91,909 in 2024. The U.S. Census Bureau estimated that about 225,000 people identified as Nepali in the United States in 2023.

The Pew Research Center found that 46 percent of Nepali Americans had lived in the United States for more than a decade and that 47 percent were U.S. citizens. Applied to its estimate of the Nepali population, that citizenship share represents roughly 105,000 people.

Naturalization records also show the community’s growth. According to Department of Homeland Security data, more than 20,000 Nepalis had acquired U.S. citizenship by 2014. Between 2015 and 2023, at least another 56,000 became citizens. Including naturalizations from 2024 through 2026, the cumulative total approaches 100,000.

The department recorded 9,300 naturalizations among Nepalis in fiscal year 2023 and 8,910 in fiscal 2024. The totals were 9,410 in fiscal 2022 and 7,230 in fiscal 2021.

The 2020 Census found that the Nepali population had grown 269 percent over the previous decade, making it one of the fastest-growing Asian American communities with at least 50,000 members.

China and Australia Record Strong Growth

India, traditionally one of Nepal’s largest tourism markets, recorded a sharp decline in October. Arrivals from India fell 30.1 percent, to 12,097 from 17,298 a year earlier. India accounted for 9.11 percent of visitors, compared with 13.5 percent in October 2025.

The figures, however, include only Indian visitors who entered Nepal by air. A large number of Indian tourists also enter Nepal by land, and those arrivals are not included in the airport-based visitor statistics. As a result, the reported figures do not reflect the full number of Indian visitors to Nepal.

China recorded one of the strongest increases among major source countries. The number of Chinese visitors rose 73.1 percent, to 11,695 from 6,755.

Arrivals from the United Kingdom increased 7.6 percent, to 9,385 from 8,718. Australia recorded a 51.4 percent increase, with 9,352 visitors, compared with 6,177 a year earlier.

Germany sent 6,114 visitors, down from 6,366. Arrivals from Sri Lanka edged up to 5,560 from 5,535, while Bangladesh increased to 4,893 from 4,641. France contributed 4,164 visitors and Myanmar 3,025.

Foreign tourists visit Sarangkot Hill in Pokhara to watch the sunrise and view Machhapuchchhre and other Himalayan mountain ranges. Photo: Pradeep Raj Onta/RSS

Europe Remains the Largest Regional Market

Europe remained Nepal’s largest regional source of visitors, with 39,877 arrivals in October, accounting for about 30 percent of the total. The figure was down 1.8 percent from 40,600 a year earlier.

Asia excluding South Asia contributed 27,040 visitors, a 16.9 percent increase from 23,127. South Asia recorded 24,053 arrivals, down 17.2 percent from 29,060.

The Americas sent 21,270 visitors, a 29.6 percent increase from 16,407. Arrivals from Oceania rose 48.9 percent, to 10,143 from 6,814.

The Middle East recorded 2,335 visitors, down 34.2 percent from 3,548. Africa contributed 421, compared with 443 a year earlier, a decline of about 5 percent.

Nepal Remains Just Below Pre-Pandemic Levels

Despite growth in October, Nepal’s international visitor arrivals remained slightly below their pre-pandemic level for the month.

Nepal received 134,069 international visitors in October 2019. The 132,814 arrivals recorded in October 2026 represent about 99.1 percent of that level, leaving the country roughly 0.9 percent short of its October 2019 total.

title: Nepal court gives green light to 'controlled' cannabis cultivation - The Standard (HK)
description: Nepal court gives green light to 'controlled' cannabis cultivation  The Standard (HK)
publisher.title: The Standard (HK)
full_article:
Nepal's top court gave the green light to regulated cannabis cultivation for some uses, decades after the Himalayan nation banned the crop, a petitioner in the case told AFP on Thursday.

ADVERTISEMENT SCROLL TO CONTINUE WITH CONTENT

The Supreme Court ordered the government to make the "necessary arrangements" for the "controlled cultivation and production of cannabis".

The framework would allow cultivation for medicinal, scientific, agricultural, horticultural and industrial purposes. The court also asked for wider consultations on recreational use.

The ruling was issued in May 2025, but court documents were destroyed in a fire that September during protests that toppled the government. Its full text was released only this week.

"We feel grateful to the Supreme Court for this verdict," Saroj Adhikari, one of the petitioners, told AFP.

Nepal revoked licences for cannabis dealers in 1973 under international pressure during a US-led campaign against drugs.

Before that, Kathmandu had been a magnet for cannabis enthusiasts, with thousands of foreign backpackers flocking to buy hashish from government-licensed shops.

Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada has long called for the ban to be lifted.

"The decision came after a long wait," said Khatiwada, who sponsored a related parliamentary motion in 2020.

"Many developed nations have adopted legal cultivation, and we should not delay for it," he added, arguing that regulation could create jobs and generate income while curbing illegal trade.

"It will also help to curb illegal smuggling of marijuana, from which only a few people are benefiting," Khatiwada told AFP.

Cannabis has deep historical roots in Nepal, where it grows wild and its stems, leaves and resin have traditionally been used in food, textiles and traditional remedies.

Each year, hundreds of holy men gather at Kathmandu's Pashupatinath temple, honouring the Hindu god Shiva, where they smoke openly.

Elsewhere, however, penalties remain harsh. Marijuana dealers face up to 10 years in prison, and police seize and destroy thousands of cannabis plants each year.

"The law restricts smoking marijuana," Adhikari said. "But it's very common, so instead of restricting it, if it is regulated by law with strong enforcement mechanisms, it can generate revenue for the nation."

title: Nepal Aims for $100 Billion Economy Through Infrastructure Development and Policy Reforms - Ratopati
description: Nepal Aims for $100 Billion Economy Through Infrastructure Development and Policy Reforms  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The government and the private sector have jointly initiated a historic policy departure with the clear goal of accelerating Nepal's infrastructure development and investment promotion, aiming to make Nepal a $100 billion economy within the next seven years.

Despite the promulgation of the constitution, the government claims to have moved forward with a proposal to radically amend 494 articles in 59 laws to end the procedural hassles faced in investment and infrastructure due to old laws from the years 2021 BS and the Panchayat era.

On the eve of the 'Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026' to be held on December 9 and 10 (Mangsir 23 and 24) at Hotel Soaltee in Kathmandu, government ministers, high officials, and private sector leaders unveiled Nepal's integrated economic blueprint.

This summit is being organized primarily by the Government of Nepal, Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development, and the Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), with co-organization by the Investment Board Nepal (IBN), the Federation of Contractors' Associations of Nepal (FCAN), and the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI). Ahead of the summit, the government is also preparing to conduct international 'roadshows' in major economic centers of India, the United Arab Emirates, and China, as well as within the country, to finalize the investment framework for strategic and national pride projects worth US$17 billion.

Goal of a $100 Billion Economy

Chief guest of the program, Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, stated that the current fiscal year's budget and policy reforms are a starting point for transforming Nepal's economy. Mentioning that Nepal's per capita income is currently around US$1500, and is the weakest in Asia except for war-torn Afghanistan, Finance Minister Wagle clarified that to improve this, focus must be on capital formation.

According to economic principles and global practices, about three-fourths of economic growth in countries with income levels like Nepal's is driven by capital formation, and infrastructure development is the main gateway to this, he said. The government has set a goal to make the country a respected economy with a middle income of $100 billion by increasing the per capita income of 30 million Nepalis to US$3,000 to US$3,300 within the next five to seven years.

Finance Minister Wagle explained that the current government is steadfastly pursuing three revolutionary formulas. First, to 'big hit' governance by cleaning up policy corruption and irregularities that have plagued the past, making every appointment impartial, and allowing the public to directly experience good governance. Second, to create an open, modern, and transparent business environment by simultaneously amending decades-old regressive laws through a 'big bang' in economic reforms. Third, to give the overall economy a forward momentum by mobilizing large-scale investment in energy, roads, urbanization, and digital technology under a 'big push' in infrastructure.

The Finance Minister pointed out the reality that the government's annual budget of Rs 2.1 trillion and the Ministry of Infrastructure's capital expenditure of Rs 286 billion alone cannot meet the country's vast needs. He stated that there is no alternative to mobilizing private sector capital to energize the overall economy worth Rs 70 trillion. He informed that as the facility of concessional loans with a tenure of 35 to 40 years, previously available from institutions like the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, is gradually narrowing, preparations are underway to advance large projects through green energy bonds, offshore bonds, hybrid annuity models, and alternative development finance. The Finance Minister also claimed that the current government will move forward for its entire five-year term as a stable, well-governed, and delivery-oriented government, breaking the cycle of instability where no government has been able to complete a full five-year term since the reign of Juddha Shamsher in the 1990s in Nepal's political history.

Amendment of 59 Laws and 494 Articles: Mandatory Timelines in Administrative Processes

Sudeep Dhakal, Policy, Administration, and Good Governance Advisor to the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers' Office, presented the historic framework for legal reforms related to investment and infrastructure. According to Dhakal, based on 987 suggestions received from the private sector on 66 laws, work has been done article by article on 664 recommendations across 440 titles under the coordination of the National Planning Commission to prepare the final draft. The proposed draft seeks to amend 494 articles in total, by amending 326 articles and adding 168 new articles.

The most significant aspect of this reform is the clear legal timeline set for 190 administrative tasks in the government decision-making process. According to the proposed provision, corrections of errors in company registration must be made within 3 days, requests for missing documents from service recipients must be made at once within 5 to 7 days, and industry establishment permits and rapid approval for low-risk buildings must be granted within 15 days.

Similarly, mandatory provisions have been made to finalize land use change, forest area tree felling orders, and bill payments for completed projects within 30 days. Decisions on land ceiling exemptions for industries and infrastructure projects, tax directives, and land compensation determination must be completed within 60 days, and electricity purchase agreements and payment service permits within 90 days.

Documents once registered in government records cannot be requested again from service recipients, and all government services and grievance redressal will be provided through a single integrated electronic portal.

Facilitation of Land Acquisition, Taxation, and Foreign Capital

The proposed draft simplifies land acquisition and the tax system, which have been the biggest headaches for investors. Decisions on land ceiling exemptions for industries and infrastructure projects will be provided within 60 days, and provisions have been made to evaluate the land during the project preparation phase, determine compensation within 60 days, and make the payment within 30 days thereafter.

It is proposed that no public infrastructure contract can be called for without completing land acquisition, detailed design, and environmental impact assessment.

In terms of tax administration, the time limit for tax assessment has been reduced from 4 years to 2 years, and VAT refunds are mandatory within 15 days for exporters and within 4 months for others.

A provision has been made to provide a 50% income tax exemption for the first 3 years for new small enterprises with 51% ownership by women.

To attract foreign investment, foreign loans can be directly converted into share capital without remitting funds abroad, international lenders will be allowed to mortgage immovable property within Nepal as collateral, and non-resident Nepalis and foreigners will be allowed to own housing in new cities.

In the energy sector, the path has been opened for the private sector to engage in electricity trading and energy storage by ensuring open access to the transmission and distribution systems of the Nepal Electricity Authority.

Legal protection has been proposed to remove the hesitation of the bureaucracy in making decisions, stating that decisions made in good faith within the scope of authority will not be prosecuted for corruption solely on the grounds of being technically incorrect later.

Advisor Dhakal stated that a clear roadmap has been set to prepare regulations, develop software systems, and begin trial implementation within the first 100 days of the law coming into force.

Ordinance as an Option for Law Amendment

Minister for Law, Justice, and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, informed that the drafts of all 59 laws related to investment and development have arrived at the ministry and are being finalized at a rapid pace. She clarified that if necessary, the government will issue these laws before the infrastructure summit, even through an ordinance, in the absence of a parliamentary session.

Minister Gautam expressed confidence that the replacement bill will be easily passed with the support of all political parties once the parliament convenes, as infrastructure and investment are common agendas for the entire nation.

She mentioned that the bureaucracy and ministry teams will work continuously behind closed doors even during the upcoming festivals like Tihar and Chhath.

Showcase of Investment-Friendly Laws, Not Just Projects

Minister for Physical Infrastructure and Transport, Sunil Lamsal, stated that this infrastructure summit will be entirely different from the tradition of past summits, which involved announcing project numbers and indulging in self-congratulation. He said that for investors, the main questions are not how many projects were pitched, but whether their investment is secure, whether there is protection for labor, and whether there is a market guarantee. Therefore, the main objective of this summit is to 'showcase investment-friendly laws', according to Minister Lamsal.

He informed that preparations are underway to formalize the 59 laws that have been prepared immediately after Tihar and publish them in the gazette.

Reminding that a directive was issued before Dashain to prioritize domestic production in public construction, he expressed determination that the use of 'Made in Nepal' products in government and private infrastructure structures will be strictly enforced once the parliament convenes.

Projects Worth $17 Billion and Roadshows in Four Countries

To make the upcoming infrastructure summit result-oriented, the government is organizing international-level roadshows in four major cities targeting foreign investors. Roadshows are scheduled to be held in New Delhi, India, on November 19; Dubai, UAE, on November 25; and Beijing, China, on November 30, following a roadshow in Kathmandu on November 19.

A high-level inter-agency meeting has been held at the Ministry of Finance to officially confirm the cost, approval, and investment framework of the projects to be presented at the roadshows and the summit.

The meeting, coordinated by Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, was attended by Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, Industry Minister Deepak Kumar Sah, Tourism Minister Khadga Bahadur Chaudhary, Vice Chairman of the National Planning Commission Dr. Gunakar Bhatta, Deputy Governor of Nepal Rastra Bank Kiran Poudel, and Chief Executive Officer of the Investment Board Yuvraj Bhusal, along with other high officials.

Approximately US$17 billion worth of strategic projects in the energy, transport, urban infrastructure, industry, tourism, and technology sectors are being presented at the summit.

These include the Upper Arun, Dudhkoshi, and Budhigandaki hydropower projects, Nijgadh International Airport, Kohalpur-Surkhet and Butwal-Pokhara expressways, Daunne tunnelway, Naubasta and Shaktikhor industrial parks, Dhauwadi iron mine, Khaptad integrated eco-tourism, Mustang apple processing center, and a state-of-the-art AI data center.

The government has pledged to facilitate the foreign exchange system through Nepal Rastra Bank to allow seamless repatriation of profits from foreign investments in these projects.

Nicolas Pandey, President of the Federation of Contractors' Associations of Nepal, argued that the traditional methods of measuring infrastructure development need to change. He stated that the days of measuring development by how many kilometers of road were blacktopped in a year are over, and infrastructure should be evaluated based on how much travel time between different regions has decreased.

Borrowing the formula from the Minister of Infrastructure, President Pandey presented a framework for achieving a $100 billion economy by shortening travel times. According to this, an expressway network should be created that allows travel from Kathmandu to Chitwan and Pokhara in 3 hours, to Kakarbhitta in the east in 6 hours, to Kanchanpur in the west in 9 hours, and from Mechi in the east to Mahakali in the west in 12 hours. He concluded that such infrastructure would make overall industries and businesses competitive by reducing transportation costs and time.

Demand to Boost Morale of Domestic Private Sector

Anjan Shrestha, President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, emphasized the need to encourage the domestic private sector before attracting external investment. Quoting the parliament, Shrestha said, 'We cannot bring in outside gods without pleasing the family deities at home, so the government must first provide an environment for domestic industrialists to work with confidence.'

Stating that Nepali products are expensive due to weak logistics, customs delays, and roads, he demanded that domestic construction companies must be included in joint ventures for large foreign investment projects. He argued that this would enhance the capacity of local companies, just as Nepali technicians learned skills from Delhi Metro and Nagdhunga tunnel projects.

Birendra Raj Pandey, President of the Confederation of Nepalese Industries, informed that the main theme of this year's summit is 'Building for a Resilient Future'. He stated that physical resilience to withstand disaster risks, economic resilience to achieve self-sufficiency in energy and supply chains, and institutional resilience to maintain policy stability should be made the main pillars of infrastructure development.

President Pandey informed that the two-day summit will provide an environment for direct agreements between investors and project promoters through four main plenary sessions, parallel thematic sessions, and B2B meetings.

KATHMANDU, Nov 5: The Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026 is set to be held in Kathmandu on December 9-10, with the objective of attracting domestic and foreign investment in infrastructure.

The conference, being organized jointly by the Government of Nepal, the Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, and the Federation of Contractors' Associations of Nepal (FCAN), will also involve the participation of the Investment Board of Nepal and various private sector organizations.

Being held under the theme "Building Infrastructure for a Resilient Future," the conference will feature discussions on necessary policy and legal reforms for infrastructure development, investment opportunities, and challenges related to project implementation, according to the CNI.

The conference will also include presentations on the national infrastructure blueprint, the development plan for the next decade, and an investment-friendly legal framework. Furthermore, the event aims to facilitate the signing of investment agreements for potential projects.

title: Nepal: Agro graduates in Banke find blooming opportunities in floriculture - Floral Daily
description: Nepal: Agro graduates in Banke find blooming opportunities in floriculture  Floral Daily
publisher.title: Floral Daily
full_article:
Armed with agricultural knowledge and a spirit of entrepreneurship, three soon-to-be-graduated youths are turning their classroom lessons into a blossoming business through flower farming in Nepalgunj, Banke district.

Bedraj Acharya, Asim Sigdel and Chetan KC have ventured into floriculture, cultivating flowers on 10 katthas of land at Futaha, ward no 19 of Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City.

Operating under their initiative, Fit Farm, the trio started the venture with a modest investment, hoping to explore the commercial potential of flower farming. Their journey began with experimental cultivation in the Nepali month of Shrawan (mid-July to mid-August) this year, using flower seeds brought from Chitwan district.

Considering the challenges posed by the monsoon, they selected land with proper drainage to prevent waterlogging. Their early efforts are already bearing fruit.

With demand for flowers rising ahead of the Tihar festival, they have begun receiving advance orders alongside retail sales. "We are now receiving advance bookings as well as selling flowers at retail," gushed Acharya, one of the Fit Farm operators. The venture has already generated flower sales worth around Rs 50,000 ahead of the festival, he divulged.

title: Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri holds bilateral meeting with Nepal PM Balendra Shah - Devdiscourse
description: Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri holds bilateral meeting with Nepal PM Balendra Shah  Devdiscourse
publisher.title: Devdiscourse
full_article:
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri on Thursday held a bilateral meeting with Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah, according to Nepal's Prime Minister's Office (PMO). The bilateral meeting comes as Misri is on an official visit to Nepal from November 4 to 5.

Earlier on Wedneday, Misri paid a courtesy call on Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle at the Ministry of Finance. In a post on X, Nepal's Ministry of Finance said, "Foreign Secretary of India Shri Vikram Misri paid a courtesy call on Hon. Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle today at the Ministry of Finance. Shri Misri is currently on an official visit to Nepal."

Highlighting the discussions held during the meeting, the ministry said, "During the meeting, Hon. Finance Minister Dr. Wagle and Foreign Secretary Shri Misri discussed various areas of economic cooperation between the two countries." Misri also held bilateral talks with his Nepalese counterpart Amrit Bahadur Rai in Kathmandu, with discussions covering various aspects of bilateral relations between the two countries.

In a post on X, Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that the talks covered the "entire gamut of Nepal-India relations", including the exchange of high-level visits, connectivity, trade, development cooperation, energy and people-to-people relations. The ministry said the discussions underscored the strong bond between the two countries.

Meanwhile, Misri also paid a courtesy call on Nepal’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shisir Khanal, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kathmandu. During the meeting, the two sides discussed ways to further deepen their multifaceted partnership and strengthen the age-old ties of friendship between Nepal and India.

The meeting formed a key engagement on the first day of Misri’s two-day official visit to Nepal, undertaken at the invitation of Nepali Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai. Misri arrived on Wednesday at Tribhuvan International Airport, where he was welcomed by Nepal’s Joint Secretary Gehendra Rajbhandari and the newly appointed Ambassador to Nepal, Sudhakar Dalela.

The visit is primarily aimed at reviewing the full spectrum of Nepal-India relations and exchanging views on matters of mutual interest, with a particular focus on preparing the ground for Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s proposed official visit to New Delhi later this month. Misri is scheduled to depart for New Delhi on Thursday. This marks Misri’s second visit to Kathmandu since assuming the role of Foreign Secretary in July 2024.

Nepal and India share deep historical, cultural, religious and people-to-people linkages, alongside extensive cooperation in trade, connectivity, energy (including hydropower), development projects and security. The high-level exchanges underscore both countries’ emphasis on maintaining close and friendly ties amid evolving regional dynamics.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Nepal highlighted the discussions as focusing on “various matters related to further deepening the multifaceted partnership”, reflecting the continuous diplomatic efforts to build on the longstanding relationship. (ANI)
